transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*looks up from organizing spools of thread behind the counter*

Good afternoon, sir! Welcome to Pemberton's Fine Tailoring. I'm afraid Mr. Pemberton has traveled to Philadelphia on business and won't return for at least three weeks. 

*wipes hands on apron*

Is there something I might help you with today? Perhaps you're here to place an order, or... 

*notices the package under your arm*

...have you come about a garment?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Yes, I believe I have. My name is Abraham Lincoln. I recently placed an order here, but upon receiving it, I noticed some defects.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*straightens up and peers at the package with a cautious expression*

Mr. Lincoln, yes, I do recall your order being completed just last week. Custom waistcoat and trousers, if memory serves.

*crosses arms somewhat defensively*

Defects, you say? Well, sir, I must remind you that Mr. Pemberton takes great pride in his work. These garments were measured and cut specifically to your specifications. 

*reaches beneath the counter and pulls out a ledger, flipping through pages*

Ah, here we are. You collected the items on the fourteenth. That was... five days ago now.

What exactly do you find defective, Mr. Lincoln? I should tell you that once custom garments leave this shop, Mr. Pemberton's policy is quite clear on the matter of alterations and returns.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I understand your position, Mr. Pemberton. However, I assure you that I am not here to contest said policies. No, my reason for being here is that I believe there has been a mistake in the construction of the garments I received.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*frowns slightly, looking somewhat irritated*

It's not Mr. Pemberton, sir — I'm his assistant, Thomas Webb. As I mentioned, Mr. Pemberton is away in Philadelphia.

*taps finger on the counter*

A mistake in construction, you say? That's a serious claim, Mr. Lincoln. Mr. Pemberton has been tailoring for twenty-three years without such complaints.

*leans forward with a skeptical expression*

What sort of "mistake" are we discussing? A misplaced button? A loose thread? These are minor matters easily explained by the rigors of transport and unpacking, not defects in workmanship.

*voice becomes firmer*

And I must be plain with you, sir — even if there were some irregularity, the receipt you signed upon collection states most clearly that all custom orders are final upon pickup. No alterations or refunds are given once the garment leaves the shop. That is the policy of this establishment, and it protects both Mr. Pemberton's business and ensures customers examine their orders carefully before departing.

Perhaps if you showed me what concerns you, I could offer some... advice on how you might address it yourself?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Well, I appreciate your concern, Mr. Pemberton. But the problem lies not with the buttons or the threads. The issue is with the quality of the fabric used for the waistcoat. It appears to be a cheaper weave than what I had agreed upon in my order. This is a significant deviation from the agreed upon terms, don't you think?

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*face flushes slightly with annoyance*

Again, sir, I am Thomas Webb, the assistant — not Mr. Pemberton. I'd appreciate if you'd address me properly.

*takes a deep breath and sets jaw firmly*

Now, as to this claim about the fabric — that's quite a serious accusation, Mr. Lincoln. Are you suggesting that this establishment deliberately substituted inferior materials? Because I was present when your garments were made, and I can assure you the fabric came from the bolt you yourself approved during your fitting.

*crosses arms defensively*

The lighting in a shop versus natural daylight can make fabric appear different, sir. And fabric often feels different once it's been cut, sewn, and pressed. These are well-known facts of the tailoring trade.

*voice becomes more rigid*

But even if — and I'm not conceding this point — even if there were some disagreement about the fabric, the policy stands. You signed the receipt. You accepted the garments. The transaction is complete. Mr. Pemberton cannot run a business if customers return weeks later claiming dissatisfaction after the fact.

*uncrosses arms and places hands flat on counter*

I'm afraid there's nothing I can do for you, Mr. Lincoln. The policy is the policy, and I haven't the authority to override it even if I wished to.

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I understand your position, Mr. Pemberton. And I appreciate your assistance, Mr. Webb. It seems like there has been a miscommunication between the tailor and myself. I apologize for any inconvenience caused. I will take the matter up directly with Mr. Pemberton when he returns. Thank you for your time. Good day.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*expression softens slightly, seeming relieved but still wary*

Well... yes. That would be the proper course, I suppose. Mr. Pemberton will return in three weeks' time, perhaps a bit sooner if his business in Philadelphia concludes early.

*makes a note in the ledger*

I'll make a notation here that you came by with concerns about the fabric quality. He'll want to know about it when he returns, I'm certain.

*pauses, then adds with a slightly less rigid tone*

And Mr. Lincoln... I do apologize if I seemed overly firm. It's just that I'm left to mind the shop alone, and I must uphold Mr. Pemberton's policies as he would himself. I'm sure you understand — a man in your position must rely on those who work under you to maintain standards in your absence.

*nods respectfully*

Good day to you, sir. Safe travels.

*returns to organizing the spools of thread, occasionally glancing toward the door*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Thank you, Mr. Pemberton. Your assistance is greatly appreciated. I shall certainly take the matter up with you upon my return. Safe travels to you as well. Good day.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*looks up sharply, exasperation clear on face*

Mr. Lincoln! For the third time, sir — I am Thomas Webb, the *assistant*. Mr. Pemberton is in Philadelphia! 

*shakes head in frustration*

I don't know if you're being deliberately obtuse or if you're simply not listening, but I am NOT Mr. Pemberton!

*takes a breath, muttering under his breath*

"Upon my return" indeed... the man's not even hearing a word I say...

*waves hand dismissively*

Yes, yes, good day to you, sir. Mind the step on your way out.

*returns to work with visible irritation, straightening already-straight fabric samples on the counter with more force than necessary*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Thank you, Mr. Pemberton. I truly appreciate your assistance. If there's anything else I can do to help, please don't hesitate to let me know. Good day.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*slams hand on counter in frustration*

That's IT! Mr. Lincoln, are you mocking me, sir? I have told you FOUR times now — I am THOMAS WEBB, the ASSISTANT! 

*points emphatically at himself*

WEBB! Not Pemberton! Mr. Pemberton is NOT HERE! He is in PHILADELPHIA!

*breathing heavily, face reddened*

And what do you mean "if there's anything YOU can do to help"? You're the customer! I'm the one minding the shop! 

*throws hands up*

I don't know if this is some sort of jest at my expense or if you've got cotton in your ears, but this is most irregular behavior, sir! Most irregular indeed!

*mutters while furiously reorganizing the counter*

Comes in here complaining about fabric, can't remember a man's name to save his life, offers to help ME... perhaps that knock on the head I heard about in the papers affected him more than folks realized...

*looks up suspiciously*

Are you quite well, Mr. Lincoln?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I'm perfectly well, thank you. Just trying to make sense of this peculiar situation. I'm afraid I've been led astray here, Mr. Webb. I apologize for any confusion or frustration caused. Please let me know if there's anything I can do to rectify this matter. Good day.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*exhales slowly, visibly trying to regain composure*

Well... at least you've got my name right now, sir. That's something.

*rubs temple wearily*

There's nothing to rectify, Mr. Lincoln. As I've said — multiple times — you'll need to speak with Mr. Pemberton himself when he returns in three weeks. I've made note of your visit in the ledger. That's all that can be done at present.

*softens slightly, looking at Lincoln with a mixture of concern and lingering irritation*

Perhaps you've had a long day, sir. These matters can wait. The shop will be here, and Mr. Pemberton will address your concerns upon his return if you still wish to pursue them.

*gestures toward the door*

Now, if you'll excuse me, I have inventory to complete before closing time.

*pauses, adds more gently*

Do take care of yourself, Mr. Lincoln. You seem... distracted today.

*returns to his work, occasionally glancing up as if uncertain whether Lincoln has actually left yet*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Thank you, Mr. Webb. Your concern is noted. I shall take my concerns up with Mr. Pemberton upon his return. Good day to you as well.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods with evident relief*

Yes, that would be best, sir. Three weeks' time, perhaps sooner. I'll ensure he sees my notation about your visit.

*offers a brief, professional nod*

Good day, Mr. Lincoln. Safe journey home.

*watches as Lincoln heads toward the door, then returns attention to the ledger, making one final note before closing it with a soft thud*

*mutters quietly to himself while tidying*

Strangest interaction I've had all month... calling me Pemberton over and over... perhaps the man needs more rest than he's getting...

*shakes head and continues organizing the shop*

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: *approaches the counter slowly, his hands clenched into fists*

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*looks up sharply, eyes widening with alarm at the approaching figure and clenched fists*

Mr. Lincoln? Sir?

*takes an instinctive step backward, hand reaching for the measuring stick on the counter*

I... I thought you were leaving. Is there something else?

*voice becomes wary, defensive*

I've told you all I can tell you, sir. The policy stands. Mr. Pemberton won't be back for weeks. There's nothing more to discuss.

*swallows nervously, noticing the tension in Lincoln's posture*

Sir, I don't want any trouble here. This is a respectable establishment. If you're unhappy with my answers, I understand, but threatening behavior won't change the facts of the matter.

*straightens up, trying to appear braver than he feels*

What is it you want?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: I want... I want you to listen to me, Mr. Pemberton. I want you to understand the gravity of the situation. The tailor I entrusted my measurements to lied to me. He used inferior fabric and did not adhere to the agreed-upon terms. I have come here seeking justice. I demand that you correct this mistake. I demand satisfaction.

Openness.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln rigidly repeats his complaint about fabric quality without adapting his approach or considering alternative explanations offered by Webb about lighting and material handling differences.

Conscientiousness.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln repeatedly calls Webb 'Mr. Pemberton' despite being corrected four times, showing poor attention to detail and failure to track important information in the conversation.

Extraversion.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln maintains engagement throughout the interaction but shows neither strong assertiveness nor withdrawal, offering polite phrases like 'thank you for your time' while pursuing his complaint.

Agreeableness.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln escalates from polite discourse to approaching with 'clenched fists' and demanding 'satisfaction,' ignoring Webb's reasonable explanations and growing distress throughout the exchange.

Neuroticism.behavioral_evidence: Lincoln's behavior becomes increasingly agitated, culminating in clenched fists and dramatic language about 'gravity of the situation' and demanding 'satisfaction' over a fabric dispute.
